979 million food-delivery orders in FY2026, up from 853 million in FY2025. Net average order value over the same stretch: ₹385 to ₹388.

Read those two together. Nearly all of that growth came from volume, not from squeezing more out of each order. Most of us would have chased the second number.

Foodiebay started in 2008 as a menu site. Useful, and capped, because a catalogue solves discovery and stops right before the transaction. The gap between "I found a place" and "my dinner is here" is where most discovery businesses stall. Zomato's answer from 2015 was to expand adjacently: ordering and delivery on top of the catalogue and brand it already had.

That meant building both sides at once. In FY2026, average monthly active restaurant partners reached 330,000 and delivery partners 552,000, with 24.3 million average monthly transacting customers. Supply and demand together, or you're running a waiting room.

The harder discipline was treating operations as part of the product. Turns out "just a directory" is a slippery phrase. An estimated delivery time is a promise. So is a menu price, and so is a refund policy. The app is just the surface of all three.

One more thing worth stealing: Zomato is a brand of Eternal Limited. Keeping the parent identity separate from the consumer brand lets each carry its own promise.

If you're a founder, pick the narrow problem you're solving first, then name the adjacent step you're already planning. What operational detail have you been tempted to skip?

# From Menu Directory to Dinner: What It Actually Took

In 2008, Foodiebay launched as a restaurant-menu discovery site. The product solved one narrow problem: finding out what a restaurant served before you showed up. Two years later it became Zomato, and the interesting part of the story starts there.

**The challenge.** A menu catalogue is a nice utility with a ceiling. Restaurants wanted orders, customers wanted the food brought to them, and neither side could get there through a website that only listed dishes. The gap between "I found a place" and "my dinner is here" is where most discovery businesses stall.

**The approach.** Zomato expanded adjacently. Discovery built the catalogue and the brand; ordering and delivery, from 2015 onward, added the transaction. That meant building both sides of the marketplace at once, with restaurant partners supplying menus, availability and preparation and delivery partners covering the last mile. Mobile apps and city-by-city expansion in the early 2010s put discovery into people's pockets first, so ordering had somewhere to land.

The harder discipline was treating operations as part of the product. An estimated delivery time is a promise, and so are a menu price and a refund policy. The app is only the surface of all three.

**The results.** FY2026 annual-report materials record 979 million food-delivery orders, up from 853 million in FY2025, with average monthly transacting customers at 24.3 million. Average monthly active restaurant partners reached 330,000 and delivery partners 552,000. Net average order value moved from ₹385 to ₹388, and order growth did the work rather than price per order.

**What founders can take.** Start with a real, narrow problem, then expand where your existing catalogue and trust give you a head start. Build supply and demand together; one without the other is a waiting room. Measure retention and unit economics, because downloads and order volume flatter you while the economics stay quiet. And keep the parent identity separate from the consumer brand, since Zomato is a brand of Eternal Limited and that separation lets each carry its own promise.

Tell us which narrow problem you're solving first and what adjacent step you're already planning. We'd genuinely like to hear it.

reasons: The argument runs on a single track. Every example points the same way and no objection is entertained.

flags: consistencyScore: The piece opens with 'FY2026' and later uses 'FY2026' again, but the brand brief uses 'FY26' and 'FY2025–26'; the fiscal-year label is not stated consistently with the source convention.

clarityScore: 'Net average order value over the same stretch: ₹385 to ₹388' — the brief labels this 'Net average order value (I)' with a currency glyph rendered as 'I'; the post silently converts it to ₹ without noting the source convention, which is a precision risk.
clarityScore: 'Most of us would have chased the second number' is a vague collective claim with no support; it reads as an unsourced generalization.

structureScore: The paragraph 'One more thing worth stealing: Zomato is a brand of Eternal Limited. Keeping the parent identity separate from the consumer brand lets each carry its own promise.' introduces a new thesis (parent/brand separation) that is not developed and sits awkwardly before the CTA.

brandScore: 'Turns out "just a directory" is a slippery phrase' is conversational but slightly muddled; the intended point (operations are part of the product) is not stated explicitly, weakening the key message.

consistencyScore: Tone shifts between analytical ('Read those two together') and instructional ('If you're a founder, pick the narrow problem...'), which is acceptable on LinkedIn but slightly uneven.

groundingScore: 'Zomato's answer from 2015 was to expand adjacently' — the brief says '2015 onward: Food ordering and delivery became a central growth engine', so the date is supported, but the framing as a deliberate 'answer' is an interpretive claim not in the brief.
clarityScore: 'Supply and demand together, or you're running a waiting room' is a vivid but imprecise metaphor that may not land for all readers.
suggestions: Use 'FY26' consistently and add a parenthetical '(year ended 31 March 2026)' on first use to match the brand brief's convention.
Replace 'Most of us would have chased the second number' with a concrete, sourced observation, e.g., 'The brief notes order growth appears more important than a large change in per-order value.'
Either develop the Eternal/Zomato parent-brand point into a full paragraph or cut it; as written it distracts from the operations-as-product thesis.
Make the key message explicit: add a sentence like 'Operations are part of the product — the estimate, the price and the refund are the product surface.'
Clarify the ₹385→₹388 figure by noting it is 'net average order value' as reported, and avoid implying it is a like-for-like currency conversion if the source uses a different glyph.
Tighten the 'waiting room' metaphor or replace it with a plain statement about balancing supply and demand.
qa.summary: A strong, well-paced LinkedIn post that grounds its argument in verified FY26 metrics and lands a clear founder takeaway, but needs tighter fiscal-year labeling, an explicit statement of the 'operations are part of the product' message, and either development or removal of the underdeveloped Eternal parent-brand point.
